newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Russia tax rises may hit Sri Lanka tea exports.
newsitem.headline: Russia tax rises may hit Sri Lanka tea exports.

text.p: An increase in Russian taxes on tea imports may hurt Sri Lankan exports of value-added tea to a key market, industry officials said on Tuesday.

"It is particularly damaging," said Anile Cooke, director of brokers Forbes and Walker. "It is unlikely in the short term to lead to a drop in our exports because of the preference for Ceylon tea. But there will be pressure on shelf prices."
Russia has said it will aise import duty and taxes on pre-packed Sri Lankan teas to 38 percent from 29 percent from June 1.
"Although it is not going to hit prices at the moment it will have a bearing on our future exports to Russia in the medium term," said Lalith Ramanayake, director of brokerage John Keells.
"It will make it hard for our value-added tea exports in the medium term."
Last year, the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) emerged as the biggest importer of Sri Lankan tea, buying almost 47 million kilos, mainly in packets, up from 40 million in 1995.
The Tea Board has said tea exported by countries like India, Indonesia, Bangladesh and Vietnam will be only subject to a 15 percent import duty because of agreements signed during the Soviet era.
Another 1.5 percent is paid in taxes on all goods imported into Russia.
"This is a huge discriminatory factor for Sri Lankan teas to compete in the Russian Federation," a Tea Board statement said.

Before April 1995 tea imports into Russia were virtually exempt from import duty and taxes, but in the past two years duty on packeted tea was raised to 10 percent and tea imports were made subject to a value-added tax of 20 percent, the Tea Board said.
Despite this, Sri Lankan tea exports to Russia and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) as a whole continued to grow, it said.

"If (Russia) continues to keep increasing taxes then exporters might have to do blending there," Ramanayake of John Keells told Reuters. "That is not a good idea. It will not help Sri Lanka's industry. It will really help multinationals to come in with branded products."
Industry officials said Russia's tax hike was probably prompted by the need for the cash-strapped economy to raise funds by taxing essential foods like tea.
Packing plants in Russia may also have demanded protection against exporters like Sri Lanka, they said.

Industry analysts say tea prices will come off last year's record highs but 1997 should still be a buoyant year due to continuing demand from the CIS and Middle East, which favour Sri Lanka's low-grown long-leaf orthodox teas.
